# Latchkey

> Your projects move; your secrets don't. Latchkey keeps API keys, database URLs and key files in iCloud Keychain;
> project files keep latchkey:// references; Latchkey fills the values in when a command starts, after the owner
> approves with Touch ID, Apple Watch or their password, or under a grant they made. For developers and the coding
> agents they run. This file is everything an agent needs to work with it; the full text of every page is at
> https://latchkey.snackstud.io/llms-full.txt.

- Platform: a Mac app, macOS 15 or later, with a command-line tool, `latchkey` (`lk` for short).
- Storage: iCloud Keychain, in Latchkey's own access group, synced to the owner's Macs. No Latchkey server or account.
- Price: free to download and use, and the core is meant to stay free. Latchkey Pro is a planned one-time purchase in the Mac
  App Store version; it isn't on sale.
- Source: https://github.com/zachshallbetter/latchkey (FSL-1.1-ALv2).
- Made by Zach Shallbetter (https://zachshallbetter.com/), a systems engineer in Spokane, Washington; published by
  his studio, Snack Studio (https://www.snackstud.io). Contact: latchkey@snackstud.io.

## Rules for agents

Put this in CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or your instructions, and follow it:

> Secrets are in Latchkey. Env files hold `latchkey://` references, not values. Run anything that needs secrets as
> `latchkey run --env-file .env.local -- <command>` or `latchkey run --env <project>/<environment> -- <command>`.
> Never run `latchkey get`, never print the environment, and never read or write values in `.env` files. If
> `latchkey` exits with 77 (refused) or 66 (missing), stop and ask; don't retry.

- Installing the app, approving reads and making grants are the person's job. Ask them; don't work around a refusal.
- `latchkey check --env-file .env.local` (or the MCP tool `latchkey_check`) shows what a run would get without
  asking, what would ask, and what's missing. Use it before a slow run.
- Never put a value in a command line, a file, a commit or a chat message. If a key is missing, give the person the
  command to add it: `latchkey set <project>/<environment>/<NAME>` (the value is read from a hidden prompt or
  standard input).

## Is it installed?

- `latchkey status` prints where values are kept, how the person approves, item and grant counts and the socket. It
  should say `storage: iCloud Keychain`.
- If `latchkey` isn't found: the person installs the app (https://github.com/zachshallbetter/latchkey/releases/latest,
  or `brew tap zachshallbetter/latchkey`, `brew trust zachshallbetter/latchkey`, `brew install --cask latchkey`, which
  adds `latchkey` and `lk` to `~/.local/bin`). With the disk image, they choose Latchkey › Install Command Line Tool….
  With the Mac App Store version, the tool is a separate download: after tapping as above, `brew install latchkey-cli`
  (https://latchkey.snackstud.io/cli.html). `~/.local/bin` must be on the PATH.
- Exit 69 means the app can't be reached: ask the person to open Latchkey.

## Running commands

```bash
latchkey run --env-file .env.local -- npm test
latchkey run --env shop/development -- npm run dev           # no env file needed
latchkey run --file ASC_KEY_PATH=shop/production/ASC_P8 -- fastlane beta   # a key file, as a temporary path
```

- References: `latchkey://ID` is replaced by the value; `latchkey-file://ID` by the path of a temporary file only the
  owner can read, deleted when the command exits.
- Output is masked: exact copies of secret values (6 characters or longer) are hidden in what the command prints.
  Transformed or encoded copies are not.
- Exit codes: 0 done; 64 wrong usage (fix the command); 66 no item with that ID (stop, ask the person to add it);
  69 app unreachable (ask them to open Latchkey); 73 a file couldn't be rewritten (stop and report); 77 refused (stop,
  ask them to approve or grant; don't retry); 127 the command couldn't start. On 66 and 77 Latchkey prints the IDs and,
  for 77, the exact `latchkey grant` command that would allow them.

## Approvals and grants

- Each read that isn't agent-safe or covered by a grant asks the person, showing the agent, the programs it runs
  through, the folder and the command. Several requests in a row from the same agent and folder share one panel and
  one Touch ID, so batching reads costs the person one touch; a refusal still means stop and ask.
- Before they step away, the person can grant what a job needs:
  `latchkey grant 'shop/development/*' --session --for 4h` (ends when the agent quits),
  `latchkey grant 'shop/development/*' --command "npm test" --for 2h` (only that command), or
  `--folder ~/Projects/shop --for 2h`. A grant for a repository's folder covers its worktrees.
- Through MCP, `latchkey_request_grant` asks the person for a grant on items in the agent's folder; it ends when the
  agent quits or after a day at most, and can't include production environments or a whole project.

## New clones and worktrees

`.env` files are gitignored, so a fresh clone or worktree has none. `latchkey project` says which project the
checkout is (from its Git remotes); `latchkey export <project>/<environment> --out .env.local` writes an env file of
references and plain settings, never values; or skip the file with `latchkey run --env <project>/<environment>`.

## Keys an agent can use but never read

- OpenAI and Anthropic: `latchkey run --proxy --env-file .env.local -- npm test` gives the command a placeholder key
  and a local base URL; the real key is added only to requests to the provider. `--proxy-models A,B` and
  `--proxy-requests N` limit which models a run may name and how many requests it may make.
- AWS: `latchkey run --aws-session` (or `--aws-role ARN`) gives the command credentials that expire after 15 minutes
  by default instead of the long-lived key; `--aws-for` sets the time, up to 12 hours.

## MCP

```bash
claude mcp add latchkey -- ~/.local/bin/latchkey mcp
```

- Tools: latchkey_status, latchkey_list (IDs, never values), latchkey_check, latchkey_run (runs a command with
  references filled in; output masked, last 64 KB of each stream; stops after 10 minutes by default, at most 60;
  `proxy`, `proxy_models` and `proxy_requests` work as on the command line), latchkey_request_grant, latchkey_project
  and latchkey_export_references. There is no tool that reads a value, exports values, changes items or pushes.
- Another MCP server started as a command can get its keys through Latchkey: wrap its command and keep references in
  its environment.

```json
{
  "command": "latchkey",
  "args": ["run", "--no-masking", "--", "npx", "-y", "some-mcp-server"],
  "env": { "SOME_API_KEY": "latchkey://SOME_API_KEY" }
}
```

## Keeping values out of files

- `latchkey import .env.local --dry-run` shows where each value would go (names and counts, never values);
  `latchkey import .env.local --rewrite` saves them with one approval and leaves references in the file. Settings
  such as PORT and NODE_ENV stay in the file; public values are saved plain; anything unclear is a secret.
- `latchkey scan --staged` lists env files a commit would add that still hold plain values (file, line and name,
  never the value) and exits 1 if there are any. `latchkey scan --install-hook` adds it as a pre-commit hook.

## What Latchkey can't do

A value released to a command is in that command's memory and environment. The command can print it to a file, send
it over the network or encode it so masking doesn't catch it. Agent-safe settings and grants decide what reaches a
command; they can't control what it does with it. Anything running as the owner can ask, which is why reads ask by
default. https://latchkey.snackstud.io/security.html covers every protection and where it ends.
